title: Differences on the nature of efficacious grace are scholastic
source_text: LXXIX. Quod vero discrimen est inter Thomistas atque Jansenium, & inter ipsos Scholae Reformatae Doctores, in explicanda natura gratiae efficacis, & definiendo qua in re illa constituenda sit, dum illam ponunt Thomistae in motione quadam virtuosa, quae est in voluntate per modum quo impetus in re quae impellitur, Jansenius in affectibus amoris & desiderii boni coelestis & spiritualis, quibus suaviter sursum rapitur animus humanus, discipuli Cameronis in potentissima mentis illuminatione & persuasione quae voluntatem & affectus secum rapit, alii in omnipotenti & efficacissima Dei operatione qua novum principium spiritualis vitae cordi hominis vocati inditur, & homo simul excitatur ad hujus vitae actus eliciendos, res est quae ad disputationem mere Scholasticam pertinet, & de qua viris doctis sic & sic loqui, & opinari licet: & quae hic plerique viri docti proferunt componenda potius quam opponenda videntur.
pass_a_gloss: LXXIX. But the difference there is between the Thomists and Jansenius, & among the Doctors of the Reformed School themselves, in explaining the nature of efficacious grace, & in defining in what it is to be placed, while the Thomists place it in a certain virtuous motion, which is in the will in the way an impetus is in a thing which is impelled, Jansenius in affections of love & of desire of the heavenly & spiritual good, by which the human mind is sweetly carried upward, the disciples of Camero in a most powerful illumination & persuasion of the mind which carries the will & affections with it, others in an omnipotent & most efficacious operation of God by which a new principle of spiritual life is put into the heart of the man called, & the man at the same time is stirred to elicit the acts of this life, is a matter which belongs to merely Scholastic disputation, & about which learned men may speak & hold opinions this way & that: & what most learned men here put forward seems to be reconciled rather than opposed.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXIX. There are differences between the Thomists and Jansenius, and among the teachers of the Reformed school themselves, over how to explain the nature of efficacious grace and in what to place it.

The Thomists place it in a certain motion with power in it, present in the will as an impetus is present in a thing that is driven; Jansenius in feelings of love and longing for the heavenly and spiritual good, by which the human soul is gently swept upward; Camero's disciples in a most powerful enlightening and persuading of the mind, which sweeps the will and affections along with it; others in an all-powerful and most effective working of God, by which a new source of spiritual life is put into the heart of the person called and he is at the same time roused to perform the acts of this life.

All this belongs to purely scholastic debate, on which learned men may speak and think one way or another; and what most learned men put forward here seems to call for reconciling rather than setting against each other.
